items.en: Newman was accompanied at a press conference by Libertarian upper house member, John Ruddick, who, like him, was also wearing a bright orange tie. Asked if Ruddick was joining One Nation, Newman, who later insisted he was not on a “recruitment drive”, said:
We haven’t had that discussion at all. John’s John, I’m me. Don’t let the orange tie fool you.

Newman, a former investment banker and trade bureaucrat, is not a Cessnock local and returned to Australia after spending 25 years working in Japan. He was quizzed on his knowledge of the electorate, fielding questions on his favourite Cessnock pub, restaurant, what he likes to order there and the name of the local footy team.

Nationals deputy leader Darren Chester asks the prime minister if he takes responsibility “for the average mortgage–holder now paying $30,000 more per year because of the 16 interest rate rises under his government.
Anthony Albanese says he does take responsibility for the two budget surpluses and budget improvements under the Labor government.
The fact that we’ve produced eight separate either budgets or budget updates – every one of which has had a savings measure in it. We take responsibility for the fact that over 260,000 Australians...
The opposition tries to interject – the PM hasn’t said he takes responsibility for the higher mortgage payments, and the Coalition are trying to back him into a corner.
It doesn’t work, Albanese opts to sit down, indicating he’s finished his answer.
Sharkie questions government over aged care funding

Independent Rebekha Sharkie is next and asks the aged care minister why the Australian National Aged Care Classification – the funding model for residential aged care – has only received a 2.55% funding increase, below inflation.

We need 10,000 new aged care beds annually, last year just 800 were added. Thousands of our elderly are stuck in hospitals waiting for an aged care bed around our nation. Minister, this is a disaster on your watch. Will you lift the ANACC funding to at least match inflation?
The aged care minister, Sam Rae, says the government increases funding to the ANACC based on independent advice.

The government sets aged care funding based on the independent advice from the independent funding authority. It provides expert [advice] to myself and Minister Butler … with a view to working out the efficient cost of delivering care.
‘Miscommunication’ over digital duty of care, Wells tells One Nation MP

Anika Wells gets another question on the DDOC, this time from One Nation’s David Farley, who asks about an issue which has strongly activated right-wing opponents of the bill – powers for regulators to establish “sockpuppet” accounts online.

Wells said such fake accounts had been used by “malevolent” actors online for nefarious purposes, but that regulators would use it for “mystery shopping” purposes, like doing research on how platforms serve up particular types of content to particular types of users.

They need to mystery shop what is happening on platforms in order to test whether the platforms are actually doing what they say that they are doing. So if they say they are asking a 14-year-old for their age, we need to test if they are actually doing that.
What the eSafety commission, or accredited researchers do, is create an account, as a 14-year-old girl, and test those hypotheses. They do it for good purposes.
We think that we should be able to mark tech platforms’ homework – they should not get to mark their own homework. So that is the purpose of sockpuppets.
Nationals MP Jamie Chaffey asks the prime minister about the federal court ruling that the government blocked a billion-dollar goldmine in central-west NSW without authority.
Anthony Albanese doesn’t want to bite – he says it’s a legal matter so won’t comment.

I understand the federal court found the declaration was not validly made. This was a complex legal case and as it’s a legal matter we will work through the judgment together with the attorney general and we’ll consider the findings very carefully indeed.
‘Magnificent, marvellous, magnetic’, the House plays a guessing game on Clare’s dixers
There’s a bit of a running joke on the education minister, Jason Clare’s, dixers.
Clare loves a bit of alliteration when thanking a backbencher for a pre-planned softball question.
Yesterday it was the “dazzling member for Deakin”.
Today the question comes from the member for Menzies, Gabriel Ng, and the opposition tries to guess the adjective as Clare steps up to the dispatch box.
They try, “magnificent”, and “marvellous”.
Clare laughs and thanks “the magnetic member for Menzies”.
‘Put your politics to the side’, Wells urges Coalition on online safety

The communications minister, Anika Wells, says Labor’s proposed digital duty of care “moves the safety net upstream” to require tech companies do better, taking a shot at the Coalition for refusing to discuss the legislation.

Wells will introduce the legislation tomorrow, then give a major speech at the National Press Club about it. She tells question time Australia already has “one of the most comprehensive online safety frameworks in the world”, but more work is needed.

“An independent statutory review has found that it is not able to cope with the growing scale of problems in the online world. Just last week, the AFP commissioner, Krissy Barrett, warned that the police cannot be the only safety net when it comes to the radicalisation of young people online. By the time the AFP is knocking on a door, the harm is already done.
She said the digital duty of care would “shift the burden from the shoulders of victims … to the companies that are creating the environments where harms occur.”
It moves the safety net upstream to the people who design the product before it ever reaches the child.
Wells said she was surprised at the Coalition’s reticence over the bill, after shadow spokesperson Sarah Henderson said the opposition wasn’t interested in negotiating.

Last week, they were criticising our online safety laws for not having enough parliamentary scrutiny. This week, they’re criticising our online safety lords for having too much parliamentary scrutiny.
Put your politics to the side, listen to the AFP commissioner, and help us pass these laws.

Independent Monique Ryan is next and asks the health minister if he can guarantee that Victorian children won’t slip through the gap under Thriving Kids – which will replace NDIS services for children under nine with low level needs.
Mark Butler says that the state delivery of the program basically mean that those jurisdictions provide some of the services they used to before the NDIS was implemented.
He concedes there will be a degree of variation between jurisdictions about the type of service and the location of that service.
But he says there will still be standards they will have to meet:

We have been very clear that there are outcomes that we expect to see, performance indicators that we expect to have met by all state and territory jurisdictions. They are incorporated into the Thriving Kids bilateral agreements that all state governments have signed.
Beau Lamarre-Condon previously visited a farm where he later tried to sink the bodies of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies, the prosecution has told a Sydney court.
The rural property belonged to the family of a man the police officer had met on a dating app and the two visited the farm together months before the alleged murders.
Lamarre-Condon, 31, has been accused of shooting dead Baird and Davies with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.
He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

The prosecution on Wednesday read out a statement from Michael Cella who was 20 years old when he spoke with police in 2024. Cella said he matched with Lamarre-Condon on the dating app Hinge in March 2023.
They began seeing each other, with the pair going to Bondi Junction to watch Hunger Games and the Taylor Swift movie in late 2023. They also ate sushi together.
In November 2023, Lamarre-Condon invited the younger man on a weekend trip to a cabin.
But because the proposed trip was too expensive, Cella invited the police officer to go to his family’s hobby farm in Bungonia.
The property had four dams, animals, a fence and a front gate with chains and a padlock, the court heard on Wednesday.

On 6 November, they drove around the area, looked at the animals and stayed overnight, with Lamarre-Condon recording the farm and posting it to his Instagram story with the Taylor Swift song You Belong With Me.
Cella later learned about Baird when he saw Lamarre-Condon’s Instagram posts with him.
“Beau told me they were friends. I sensed there was something more and Beau was not telling me everything,” Cella said in his 2024 statement read to the jury.
Communication between Lamarre-Condon and Cella slowed significantly about mid-November 2023 and the latter soon lost interest.
He received some messages from Lamarre-Condon in January 2024 but ignored them, blocked his contact number and deleted their text message conversation, the court heard.
Days later, he received a call from a number with no called ID and did not answer, followed by a message on the encrypted messaging app Signal from a contact with the name Bob. Cella did not respond.
After the deaths of Baird and Davies, Lamarre-Condon allegedly made an unsuccessful attempt to sink their bodies at the bottom of a dam at Cella Farm, the prosecution has told the jury.
They were later found at the fence line of a monastery about 20km from the property.
The defence has not disputed the officer attempted to clean up the scene or dispose of the bodies, claiming he “panicked considerably” after acting in self-defence.
But the events inside Baird’s home are contested.
The defence has argued the couple were accidentally shot in two separate struggles.
The prosecution has told the court that Lamarre-Condon shot Baird twice in the kitchen before shooting Davies through a bedroom door.
A computer-generated video outlining the crown’s version of events was played to the New South Wales supreme court jury earlier on Wednesday.

The 3D recreation of the Paddington terrace on the morning of the shootings allowed the jury to see the path Lamarre-Condon allegedly took through the home. The reconstruction included photos of bullet holes and marks.
The potential trajectory of the bullets was also highlighted.
Before the video was shown, justice Natalie Adams said it was the crown case that Baird was shot at close range but the defence argued he was shot from further away.
The judge warned the kitchen was not shown to scale and that not all the evidence relevant to the angle or distance of the shot to Baird’s head had been adduced.
The NSW police firearms examiner, Lucas Van Der Walt, said he was more certain of the trajectory of the bullet through the bedroom door because it had passed through 35mm thick wood.
Van Der Walt told the court that “stippling” had been found on the door around a bullet hole that the prosecution alleged was covered with putty and a plastic hook.
Stippling is the pattern made by gun shot propellant particles. The closer a target is to a barrel, the smaller the spread pattern would be, Van Der Walt said on Wednesday.
“[It] is going to pepper itself into that softer surface – in this case a painted door,” he told the jury.
The court was shown a video of police taking the door from Baird’s bedroom and shooting it with the same gun and ammunition that was allegedly used by Lamarre-Condon.

The pictures of both the original and test bullet hole were compared and shown to the jury. Van Der Walt said there was a “very similar spread pattern of the propellant particles impacting with the paint and the wood in the door”.
He suggested the muzzle of the firearm was 10 to 20cm away from Davies when it was discharged.
On the side of the door the bullet would have exited, he noted the splintering looked more opaque in the original hole, but he said that was because wood putty had been used to fill the hole.
Defence lawyer John Stratton SC suggested the bullet hole could have been created if there was a body in front of the door, but Van Der Walt said the “clear stippling” would prevent that scenario.
Asked why there was no other bullet marks or bullets found in the room, the expert said it could have hypothetically hit a pillow, jacket or similar item.
“If that bullet continued and penetrated any of these surfaces and that object was removed and discarded, we’ll never find that bullet,” he told the court.
Bullets shot in this way fell to the ground, he said, and given the scene had been cleaned extensively, a casing could have been picked up by cleaners, Van Der Walt told the jury.
The trial before justice Adams continues.

Council red tape is stymieing the right to protest, a report has said, after a regional New South Wales council told a protest organiser they needed a $20m public liability insurance policy to hold a rally in a park.

A report released on Wednesday, co-authored by Australian Democracy Network (ADN) and Deakin University’s Centre for Law as Protection, raised concerns about incidents in which councils have required protest organisers to obtain insurance when rallies are held on council land.
It also expressed concern about the power some regional and urban councils have to issue financial penalties if public gatherings are held without a council permit.

In July, Mariella Gussoni notified Bathurst regional council she was holding a protest in a local park against the culling of brumbies in Kosciuszko national park. In her email to the council, seen by Guardian Australia, she said the protest would be part of nationwide rallies on a set day in August. The protest would include speakers and music, and she wasn’t sure if five or 50 people would attend, she wrote.

The council responded by letter, seen by Guardian Australia, saying it would permit her to hold her planned protest on the condition she take out a $20m public liability insurance policy, noting the council would not be liable for any loss or injury.

Nervous about what that could mean, and how much it would cost, the 61-year-old decided to hold the protest, which was attended by an estimated 120 people, next to the park. She notified police of her intention to hold the rally on the footpath – which is not council land – and said it went ahead without any issues.
“It scared me that I would be liable,” she said. “I had just let the council know as a courtesy.”
A spokesperson for Bathurst council said: “Council engaged with the event organisers at the time and won’t be providing any further comment on the matter.”

Report co-author and ADN protest rights campaigner, Anastasia Radievska, said council red tape such as insurance requirements could have a chilling effect on people speaking up about what’s happening in their local neighbourhoods.
“Often, community groups might spring up in relation to a specific local issue,” she said. “The more councils do this, the more other councils think that this is the way to interact with protest.”

The report said that across most Australian jurisdictions, “protest is unlawful or unprotected” without “permission from police, councils or place managers” and called for existing permit systems to be considered a process of notification rather than authorisation. It also recommended there be no insurance requirements.

NSW carries a $2,200 fine if a public gathering is held on council land without a permit, the report noted. This is a default requirement under the Local Government Act, but some councils have their own policies which deviate from the act. The city of Sydney has passed a number of motions affirming the right to protest on council land.

This requirement exists in addition to the police’s form 1 process, in which protesters can notify police of an intention to protest and gain immunity from being charged for offences such as obstructing a road in a designated area.
Tim Roberts, the president of the Council for Civil Liberties, said council demands for insurance or permits were “unhelpful” and a “reactionary approach”.
“It’s a blatant contravention of the right to protest,” Roberts said, referring to the implied right to freedom of political communication in the Australian constitution.

He agreed that protest organisers should only be required to give notice and not seek authorisation. He equated the council requiring insurance with calls for a user-pays system for the policing of protests.

Last week, a community group opposing a proposed $2.9bn datacentre on Sydney’s Cooks River was told by Bayside council it needed public liability insurance to hold a rally at Cahill Park in Wolli Creek.

The council also told the organisers it required an event application because their event included food, a film, and amplified sound. One of the organisers for Stop the Cooks River AI Project (SCRAP), Caitlin Boyce, said the council said it would need eight weeks to assess the application.

After receiving pro bono legal advice, the group decided to take their chances and go ahead with the protest without making an event application to the council. Boyce said she hasn’t heard from the council since going ahead with the rally.

A spokesperson for the Bayside council said it was not opposed to the public gathering, but the planned activities – which it said included a barbecue and smoking ceremony – “constitute an organised event and are subject to Council’s event approval requirements”.
Local Government NSW and the Office of Local Government were approached for comment.
The American League Championship Series has pitted two of the most unlikely franchises against each other, with a trip to the World Series on the line.

The Tampa Bay Rays entered the 2026 season with one of the three lowest payrolls in baseball, as they usually do. They made few big additions, preferring to trust their farm system, player development staff, and the ability to mix and match players in specific situations.

Meanwhile, the Cleveland Guardians found a way to reduce spending even further, running the lowest payroll in Major League Baseball, in order to maximize profits for team ownership. Fast-forward to October, and the Rays and Guardians are the two AL teams, not the Yankees or Red Sox. Not the Astros and Rangers from big markets in Texas. Or the Blue Jays, with their top-5 payroll, or even Detroit, where the Tigers ran the 11th highest payroll in baseball and by far the highest in the AL Central.
As surprising as it comes, if you haven't watched baseball before. But maybe even more surprising? How game one of the ALCS between these two teams played out.

Cleveland, hardly known as an offensive powerhouse, fell behind 2-0 against one of the best run prevention teams in baseball. Then, starting in the sixth inning, they started scoring and never stopped. Home runs from Chase DeLauter and light-hitting catcher Patrick Bailey tied it, and a parade of hits led to a 4-3 lead in the eighth, which they promptly expanded to 7-3 by the ninth.

The team that finished 24th in the league in runs scored, exploding for seven runs in game one of the ALCS against one of the best pitching staffs in baseball. If that doesn't demonstrate the randomness of postseason baseball, it's hard to know what does.

That set up what amounts to a must-win situation for the favored Tampa Bay Rays in game two, who sent midseason trade addition Freddy Peralta, acquired from the lowly New York Mets, to the mound hoping to even the series. Cleveland countered with Parker Messick, coming off an outstanding season of his own. But on Tuesday, Peralta, despite his struggles in New York, was electric.

Six shutout innings, with six strikeouts and just four hits allowed, with an average fastball velocity over 2.5 mph higher than his season average. And he got a little help from his defense too, as star third baseman Junior Caminero made a nice play on a liner to his left, and hit the Dikembe Mutombo finger wag afterward.
Just as you'd expect from the Tampa pitching lab, Peralta's start lowered his ERA to just 0.81 over his last eight starts in a Rays uniform. Somehow, they do it every single time.

On offense, the Rays' lineup got to Messick in the fourth thanks to some shaky Cleveland defense. After Victor Mesa Jr. beat out an infield single, overturned on review, Jonny DeLuca struck out and Ben Williamson hit what seemed to be a routine grounder to third. But it took a funny hop and got through Guardians third baseman José Ramírez, scoring Mesa from third. Then Liam Hicks made it really hurt, lacing a line drive single to center to score Williamson and Chandler Simpson and extend the lead to 3-0.

The Guardians, as has become their trademark of late, battled back in the seventh. Patrick Bailey worked a leadoff walk after an ABS challenge, and got to second on a one-out Steven Kwan single. After José Ramírez flew out, Chase DeLauter drove in a run with a 105mph double to right. With the tying run at second base, Cleveland sent up Jo Adell, another impactful midseason acquisition who helped seal the game one win with a two-run single in the ninth inning. But Ian Seymour shut the door, getting Adell swinging on a changeup out of the zone.

The Guardians couldn't get anything going in the eighth, and Tampa went into the ninth inning with their dominant closer, Bryan Baker, looking to finish it out. And he did on just seven pitches, going through a quick 1-2-3 inning to even the series at a game apiece.

Tampa entered the series as big favorites, thanks to their deep pitching staff, and a lineup that's better as a whole than the sum of its parts. Plus Baker, who's followed up his 1.44 ERA in the regular season with four scoreless innings and four saves in the playoffs.

Tuesday's game two was a microcosm of this year's postseason; dominant pitching and timely, often advantageous hitting. Given these two teams' strengths, that's likely to continue for the remainder of the series.

The ALCS now shifts to Cleveland for game three, where Gavin Williams, coming off a dominant ALDS start against the White Sox, is expected to face Tampa bulk pitcher Griffin Jax. Expect a raucous crowd at Progressive Field, as the Guardians look to make progress towards a return to the World Series for the first time since 2016.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Tuesday he has "no plans" to fire NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch, pushing back against calls from his democratic socialist allies to remove the city's top cop following protests over an ICE-involved shooting in the Bronx.
Ahead of a ceremony Tuesday honoring fallen NYPD officers, Mamdani was asked about Tisch's future as head of the department.
"Jessica Tisch is the police commissioner. I have no plans to change that," Mamdani told reporters.

"The reason that I made the decision to have Jessica Tisch as the police commissioner was because of her record of uprooting corruption from the upper echelons of the NYPD while lowering crime across our city," he continued. "And over the last 10 months that we've worked together, we have delivered the lowest recorded number of murders in our city's history, the lowest recorded number of shootings as well as shooting victims."

The mayor's comments came after the New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) called for Tisch's removal following last week's ICE shooting and demanded that Mamdani use his authority to drive ICE out of New York City.
The demand followed last week's shooting of Oscar Belgal during a federal immigration operation in the Bronx.

According to the Department of Homeland Security, Belgal, a 28-year-old Dominican national, was shot after allegedly refusing to comply with officers' orders during a targeted ICE operation to arrest him.
Following the incident, a City Hall spokesperson said Mamdani was reviewing the circumstances surrounding the shooting but had no plans to remove Tisch.

Scott Munro, president of the Detectives' Endowment Association — the union representing active and retired NYPD detectives — was also asked by reporters Tuesday about the DSA urging Mamdani to fire Tisch.
Munro said he believes Mamdani supports the police commissioner, noting that crime was down and Tisch was "doing her job."

Mamdani and Tisch appeared together Tuesday at the New York City Police Memorial, where they honored 42 fallen NYPD members, including 41 who died from illnesses related to the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks and their aftermath. The ceremony also honored Detective First Grade Didarul Islam, who was killed in a Midtown Manhattan mass shooting in 2025.
The mayor paid tribute to the fallen officers and their families during the ceremony, which Tisch also attended.
"While we cannot feel the silence they left behind, we will refuse to let their memory fade," Mamdani said.
Earlier this week, Mamdani directed the NYPD to conduct a comprehensive review of its use-of-force policies and practices.
He also announced reforms aimed at strengthening accountability when police officers are accused of serious misconduct.
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts probably never thought he'd have to take Shohei Ohtani out of his lineup during a postseason series. Ever.
But after the team went down 2-0 in the NLCS to the Milwaukee Brewers, with Ohtani struggling at the plate, a decision had to be made heading into Game 3 at Dodger Stadium.
The final verdict? Roberts will be trusting his Japanese superstar.

"He’s adamant he feels good enough to be in there," Roberts told reporters, via The New York Post, during the team’s off-day on Tuesday regarding Ohtani’s left knee and right arm ailments he’s been dealing with. "He’s close to finding something with his swing. I feel great about it."

Ohtani has been serving as the Dodgers’ designated hitter, but he has been slumping throughout the postseason. His batting average is now down to a measly .150 after going 0-for-4 with two strikeouts in the Game 2 loss to the Brewers in Milwaukee. He also hasn’t had an extra-base hit or an RBI in the playoffs.
It was Roberts who started the debate over whether Ohtani should be in the Game 3 lineup after his postgame comments on Monday night to The Athletic.
Roberts ultimately decided the four-time MVP should get another shot after having a meeting with president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman and general manager Brandon Gomes.
"He was very convicted that he is onto something mechanically," Roberts added. "He was adamant that he can help us, he’s well enough to help us win a baseball game. So, that’s all I needed to hear."
Ohtani, through his interpreter Will Ireton, added: "The symptoms shouldn’t be the reason why I can’t hit. He said he takes "full responsibility" for how he’s played thus far in October.
Ohtani’s injuries are ones he’s dealt with throughout the regular season, with his arm requiring an injured list stint to try and get better.
But it’s clearly stymied the slugger, who hasn’t hit a home run since Aug. 18 – a stretch Ohtani is not used to.
Roberts noted that his confidence in Ohtani has "never wavered," and his Game 3 decision is a testament to that.
Will it work out in a game that feels like a must-win to get momentum back on the side of the back-to-back World Series champions?
How will a diesel deal with Russia impact the U.S. market?
The price of diesel hit an all-time high in the U.S. in September. Can President Trump's deal for Russia to release more diesel onto the market bring the price down?

OK, there are plenty of legal and political questions surrounding President Trump's deal to get Russia to release more oil to the U.S. and global markets. And, of course, a lot of Americans are wondering how that deal could affect the price of diesel. NPR energy reporter Willa Rubin joins us now to talk about all of this. Hi, Willa.
CHANG: Hi. OK, so give us the lay of the land here. What is happening with the price of diesel in the U.S. right now?

RUBIN: Well, it hit an all-time high a few weeks ago, which is important for the U.S. economy. You know, our industrial supply chain relies on diesel, tractors that farmers use, trucks that bring your food from farms eventually to the grocery store. If diesel is expensive, that contributes to the price of everything that you buy. Now, the price of a gallon has come down a little bit since that September high. On average, it's now $6.27, according to AAA, but that is still really high. Diesel is about $2.60 more than this time last year.
CHANG: OK, and explain this to me. What did President Trump say about how he expects this deal would work exactly?

RUBIN: Yeah, so in a post on Truth Social on Friday, President Trump said that Russia had agreed to release 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and to global markets immediately. But, like, is that a little or a lot in terms of how much the U.S. actually uses?
RUBIN: Yeah. So to put this in context for the rest of October, Will O'Neil is an analyst at S&P Global Energy. He's a follower of all things diesel.
WILL O'NEIL: Because I could even do some quick Excel math. So 300,000 tons over the course of 20 days is...
RUBIN: I love that you broke out an Excel spreadsheet mid conversation (laughter).
O'NEIL: That's what I do. That's my job.

RUBIN: So he figured out that if you convert tons to barrels and the U.S. uses up to 4 million barrels a day, the entire amount expected to be released in October adds up to about half the diesel the U.S. uses in just one day.
RUBIN: Drops in the bucket. And if you do some more math using the entire amount expected to be released over the coming months, O'Neil said it adds up to about nine days' worth.
CHANG: Let me ask you this. Is Russia really in any position to export all of this diesel?
RUBIN: Analysts in the U.S. don't know, but what...
RUBIN: ...They do know is that Russia's refinery capacity has been significantly reduced by Ukraine's strikes. O'Neil says it's probably reduced 40- to 45% of their capacity.
O'NEIL: Ukrainian drone strikes have taken so much of its refining capacity offline that it just simply doesn't have the diesel production to send to global markets.

RUBIN: He says this deal does not change that reality. Russia has had an export ban since July, though they partially lifted it on Saturday. Also worth noting, the U.S. has had wide ranging sanctions on Russian energy since its full scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. On Friday, the Treasury Department announced it was temporarily waiving sanctions on diesel for about six months. And this has gotten some pushback from members of Congress on both sides of the aisle. This is a really complicated situation, Ailsa, with a lot of moving parts.
CHANG: Clearly. OK, if Russia really can bring this diesel to market, could that help lower prices in the U.S., you think, eventually?

RUBIN: Big picture, what drives diesel prices is global demand. And there's a global diesel deficit right now. A good chunk of that is due to the war in Iran. Claudio Galimberti is a partner and chief economist at Rystad Energy. He says the world is missing up to 1.5 million barrels per day that normally come from the Middle East and another million barrels that would come from Russia.
CLAUDIO GALIMBERTI: So it's a huge gap, and this deal only address (ph) a very small portion of that.
CHANG: OK, Willa, I'm no economist, but it sounds like he doesn't think this will really lower prices all that much. Am I getting that right?
RUBIN: Yeah. Analysts told me we will only start to see big meaningful drops in prices by solving these bottlenecks by ending the wars.
CHANG: That is NPR's Willa Rubin. Thank you so much, Willa.

Trump's diesel deal with Putin angers Europe
President Trump's diesel deal with Russia sparks European fury, as Ukraine's President Zelenskyy questions Washington's motives and allies vow to keep pressure on Moscow.
Leaders in Europe do not like President Trump's latest moves in the war in Ukraine.

Yeah. Trump demanded that Ukraine stop its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Trump also said that there was a ceasefire on attacks against energy infrastructure, which neither Ukraine nor Russia seem to know about. The president also lifted sanctions on Russian diesel fuel, even as Europeans impose new sanctions on the Russian military complex.
INSKEEP: Teri Schultz is following all this from a European security conference in Warsaw, Poland. Welcome.
INSKEEP: So what is it about the president's statements that concerns allies of Ukraine?

SCHULTZ: I think there's just really no faith in these moves by the White House, Steve. You know, President Zelenskyy spoke here remotely in Warsaw and said that even as this ceasefire was announced by President Trump, Ukrainian oil refineries were being bombed. So European officials and experts treated this basically as one more attempt by the White House to pressure Ukraine in favor of Russia. Now, one of the strongest reactions came from Trump's former Ukraine envoy, Keith Kellogg, who shared what he would advise Zelenskyy to do in quite colorful language.

KEITH KELLOGG: I'd burn down every one of the goddamn refineries that Russia has today. Take them all out. And I said (ph), you make them pay the price. You take it home. It's a military target. Take those targets out.
SCHULTZ: Now, Kellogg left his position in January and has been pretty outspoken about his support for Kyiv since.

INSKEEP: OK. So how are Europeans responding to this other development? The United States has very high diesel fuel prices, and the president suddenly announced an agreement of some sort for the U.S. to buy diesel fuel from Russia.

SCHULTZ: More of the same from the European perspective, but in the meantime, the European Union even intensified its efforts to stem the Kremlin's war effort. Now, it takes a long time to tee up sanctions, so this is not in reaction specifically to these latest U.S. moves, but the EU just imposed its largest-ever package of sanctions against almost 1,600 individuals and companies related to Russia's military industry. And while it appears that no one knew in advance about Trump's diesel deal, analyst Majda Ruge from the European Council on Foreign Relations says it wasn't exactly a surprise.
MAJDA RUGE: Trump's personal desire for economic reset with Russia and announcing business deals has really been the only consistent element of Trump's Russia-Ukraine policies.
INSKEEP: Let me come back to this security conference where you're at. What are NATO officials saying, the North Atlantic alliance?

SCHULTZ: Well, there's a lot of concern in Europe about U.S. plans to withdraw troops and military assets. So U.S. Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich - he's NATO's supreme allied commander Europe - used this conference to make sure there's no misunderstanding in Moscow that NATO's resolve is weakening. He unveiled what he called the theory of victory, describing how NATO would use its entire range of capabilities to respond to any attack.

China and North Korea will officially open the New Yalu River Bridge to traffic on Thursday, China’s state-run Xinhua news agency reports.

China completed its side of the bridge in 2014, hoping to boost trade ties. However, North Korea left its side unfinished for years as relations soured after Beijing supported United Nations sanctions over Pyongyang’s nuclear tests.
The first bridge connecting Russia and North Korea also opened earlier this month.

China’s exports to North Korea rose to a six-year high of $2.3bn last year, a 25 percent increase from the previous year. Chinese President Xi Jinping was welcomed in Pyongyang in June for the first time since 2019.
Since 2018, Beijing has tried to repair ties with Pyongyang, which also briefly began improving relations with Washington around the same time.

The China-North Korea relationship was forged during the Korean War. In 1961, the two countries signed the Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance, which remains China’s only formal military alliance.
The treaty contains a mutual defence clause committing either side to assist the other if one comes under armed attack.

Although China was North Korea’s main diplomatic partner and protector for decades, relations strained after Beijing in 2017 supported tightening sanctions on Pyongyang for its nuclear weapons programme.
Analysts say North Korea’s recent growing relationship with Russia may have changed the balance of Pyongyang’s diplomatic dependence, reducing its reliance on Beijing.

North Korea and Russia signed a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty in 2024, including a mutual defence provision. Military and political ties between the two countries have grown considerably stronger, with North Korea deploying thousands of troops to fight in Russia’s war on Ukraine.

United States President Donald Trump also signalled an interest in repairing relations with Pyongyang last month, after his talks with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un abruptly ended in 2019. In his second term, Trump has floated meeting Kim again, though no official meeting has been set.
North Korea has not yet resumed issuing tourism visas to Chinese citizens, who once made up the bulk of its overseas visitors.
While North Korea’s trade with Russia largely involves military supplies, exchanges with China could arguably involve goods North Korea needs to develop its civilian economy, analysts have said.
Singapore’s economy grew more than 5 percent in the most recent quarter, continuing an AI-fuelled boom that has made the city-state one of the fastest-growing advanced economies.

Gross domestic product (GDP) grew 5.4 percent year-on-year between July and September, down from a 6.2 percent expansion in the second quarter, according to advance government estimates released on Wednesday.
Manufacturing, which is dominated by the city-state’s semiconductor industry, grew 7.5 percent, according to the estimates from the Ministry of Trade and Industry.

Increased output in “electronics, precision engineering, transport engineering and general manufacturing clusters” drove growth, the ministry said, offsetting declines in the chemicals and biomedical sectors.
Construction, including AI-related investments such as data centres, expanded 8.8 per cent, according to the figures.
Despite the heady expansion, Singapore’s central bank left its monetary policy settings untouched in its latest announcement on Wednesday, citing expectations that AI demand will cool in 2027.
The Monetary Authority of Singapore, which manages monetary policy through currency exchange rates rather than interest rates, said it expected core inflation to average 1.5–2.0 percent in 2026.

“Global AI-driven growth is expected to ease in the latter half of next year from its current exceptional pace, while higher interest rates, amid elevated inflation in the advanced economies, would weigh on final demand growth,” the central bank said in a statement.
Singapore is a major global player in the booming chip sector, a position that has helped it weather choppy economic conditions, including the energy shock prompted by the US-Israel war on Iran.
The Southeast Asian city-state accounts for roughly 10 percent of global semiconductor output and 20 percent of semiconductor equipment production, according to government figures.

Yeow Hwee Chua, an assistant professor of economics at Nanyang Technological University, described Singapore’s economic performance as “impressive for a high-income economy, especially given the uncertain global environment”.
“The global technology investment boom has been an important driver,” Chua told Al Jazeera.
“Strong demand for electronics has supported manufacturing and related wholesale trade, illustrating how Singapore benefits from its position in global supply chains,” he said.
Singapore’s economy is expected to grow 5 percent in 2026, according to the IMF’s latest economic forecast, faster than any other advanced economy except Taiwan.
The city-state’s GDP grew 5 percent in 2025, its second straight year of growth above 5 percent – the first such streak since 2010 and 2011.

The diesel deal between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin has sparked anger in Ukraine. Under the agreement, Moscow is allowed to supply Russian diesel fuel to global markets. The US news website Axios reported the move came in response to Kyiv's failure to comply with Washington's demands to stop attacks on oil refineries in Russia.
Trump also declared that it was time "for Ukraine to get a new president."
The agreement to sell diesel was announced while talks between Ukrainian, US and European representatives were taking place in Miami.

"I think our team is simply being used as a cover. That is definitely not fair," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists shortly afterwards, describing Trump's decision as "a weak decision by strong partners."
This is hardly Kyiv's first crisis in its relationship with the Trump administration. In February 2025, Trump told Zelenskyy in the Oval Office "you don’t have the cards."

The White House confrontation was followed by a suspension of weapons deliveries and intelligence-sharing agreements. According to media reports, US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner threatened to suspend intelligence sharing during the talks in Miami, too, citing Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries as the reason. US officials have denied the reports.

The current tension recalls the dispute in the White House at the time, says Mykhailo Honchar of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies "Strategy XXI" in an interview with DW. However, he says there is no reason for Ukrainians to panic.

"Last year, too, there were threats and suspensions of intelligence sharing, as well as disruptions in weapons supplies," he said. "Then the Americans realized how much this was hurting them, too, and reluctantly resumed everything."

All the experts interviewed by DW see a connection between Trump's threats toward Ukraine and the US midterm elections on November 3. In the midterms, all seats in the House of Representatives and roughly one third of Senate seats are up for election.
Ivan Us of the National Institute for Strategic Studies in Kyiv expects a crushing defeat for the Republicans. He says the main reason will be high fuel prices.

"Donald Trump wants desperately to distract attention from the fact that high prices are linked to his war with Iran and the problems in the Strait of Hormuz. He needs a scapegoat for this. And he has decided that Ukraine will be it," the expert said.
Mykhailo Honchar sees Russia as the main beneficiary of Trump's deal with Putin: "This whole diesel deal looks like a disguised request from Putin to Trump to exert influence on Ukraine."

Honchar also links the agreement to a possible sale of the foreign assets of Russian oil company Lukoil. According to The New York Times, potential buyers of these assets include investors with ties to Trump.
Oleksandr Kraiev of the Ukrainian think tank Ukrainian Prism warns against taking drastic action.

"Slamming the door in anger will certainly not help us. In that case, security assistance and intelligence sharing will be off the table. We cannot afford that. It may be difficult, and sometimes even repulsive, but we have to maintain contact with the Americans," the expert said.

At the same time, Ukraine could work with Germany, Denmark, the United Kingdom and France to make deliveries of Russian diesel fuel "simply unrealistic." After all, the tankers would have to pass through these countries' territorial waters on their way to the United States, and the partners have already said they would not allow this.
Ivan Us advises against reading too much into the harsh rhetoric.
"You can say whatever you want in public, as long as you carry on as before," he said of the possible relationship between Kyiv and Washington.

Ukrainian diplomats should work with US Republicans and the MAGA movement. Trump's agreement with Putin is already being criticized in those circles, with some raising concerns that Russia could use the proceeds from the diesel trade to support Iran.

Us also does not rule out a legal challenge to Trump's decision. Republican Senator Tom Tillis told NBC that the president was likely violating a 2022 law prohibiting imports of Russian oil and other energy products.
Ivan Us considers US threats to cut Ukraine off from intelligence or weapons to be little more than "fearmongering" ahead of the elections.
"The US makes such statements not because it intends to take action, but to make the markets believe that it is about to exert pressure and thereby drive prices down," Us said.

The three experts agree that Kyiv should ride out the situation until after the US midterm elections on November 3. Oleksandr Kraiev says he is sure that Trump may back down on this issue after the elections, since abandoning Ukraine would mean showing weakness toward China.

Mykhailo Honchar points out that Trump's deal with Putin is already being criticized by Republicans in both the Senate and the House of Representatives. In addition, Republican Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick has introduced a bipartisan bill named after former US President Ronald Reagan that would block purchases of Russian oil.

"Despite all the threats, and perhaps even some attempts to impose temporary measures against Kyiv, it is unlikely that Trump will go any further. The situation should not be portrayed in apocalyptic terms," Honchar said.
He added that Trump's pressure was also bringing Ukraine and its European partners closer together.

India's Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) may have anticipated pushback from the government after its first round of protests in July, but the scale of barricading and detentions that greeted its leaders in a fortress-like New Delhi on October 10 was unlike anything they had anticipated.

The CJP began as a satirical online movement after the chief justice of India, Surya Kant, referred to unemployed young people as "cockroaches" in an offhand remark. The name is an ironic riff on the name of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

In its latest round of agitation, they are demanding the resignation of the country's controversy-hit Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, after more than 130 million names were reportedly removed from electoral rolls nationwide.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, accompanied by co-conveners Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, was detained from the plane in which he landed in the national capital on Saturday.

Meanwhile, police were stationed outside the homes of several other faces associated with the movement, including social media personality Dhruv Rathee, who has nearly 20 million followers on Instagram.

In central Delhi, buses were loaded with protesters, many of whom were taken to far-flung centers, where they were kept for hours. According to local media, at least 3,000 people were detained across the city.
How the government is handling the protests
The protests come as Modi marks 25 uninterrupted years leading elected governments, first in Gujarat state as chief minister and then as prime minister of India.

Ironically, "this celebration has happened at the time when he's politically at his weakest," Delhi-based writer Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay told DW. Mukhopadhyay is the author of Modi's 2013 biography "Narendra Modi: The Man, The Times."

He contrasted the government's current response with its approach in July, when thousands of young protesters took to the streets to demand the resignation of Modi's education minister over repeated exam paper leaks.
At the time, authorities had used batons, detentions and pellets to disperse the crowds gathered in central Delhi, which had been on the streets for days.

This time, authorities shifted to mass security deployments and preemptive action on a large scale. This included notices to those associated with earlier protests, transport cuts, the internet cutoff and airport arrests.

"The government has learned from its previous experience. They didn't allow people to sit at Jantar Mantar for any length of time, so it couldn't balloon," Pearl Pandya, senior analyst for Asia at global monitor ACLED, told DW.

"What's worrying is whether this becomes a playbook for the future — that you are not allowed to protest in the first place," she added, referring to the government's decision to remove the 18th-century observatory Jantar Mantar in central Delhi from the list of designated protest sites.
Authorities, however, have announced three new designated protest sites in the national capital.
Mukhopadhyay had a different reading of the situation. "The scale of this deployment is actually a defeat for Mr. Modi," he said.
Mukhopadhyay argued that it was already a setback for the government if it was forced to deploy security forces on such a scale in response to protests from a completely new socio-political movement.
Despite the momentum, the CJP has not been able to replicate its success from July, with the protests against Kumar being led primarily by opposition leaders and student organizations.
"Education was far more of a cross-cutting issue... the right to vote is still seen as an intrinsically political one, where it's the opposition versus the BJP," Pandya said.
The CJP, however, has long maintained that it is non-political. This is often cited as the reason for them amassing such a large following of young followers.
Mukhopadhyay criticized that stance, saying: "You cannot raise issues about electoral neutrality... without saying that these are political issues."
Despite the differences between the previous round of CJP protests in July and the current wave of demonstrations, sociologist Surinder Singh Jodhka emphasized continuity.

"I don't think they're qualitatively different. Once again, young people are the ones who are mobilized, and they are much more encouraged because the earlier round of protests was successful," he told DW. "And it's also asking similar questions about institutions, about democracy, about transparency and accountability."
"There is a new hope for those who had earlier given up on India, and felt like the right wing was in complete control," Jodhka added.

Dismissing comparisons with volatile protests in neighboring Nepal and Bangladesh, which brought down their governments, the analysts pointed to India's strong institutions as a safeguard against a dramatic change of government.

"India has had a very strong state system and state institutions," Jodhka explained, highlighting that even the opposition parties were asking for "the revival of institutions, rather than an overthrow of the state."
Pandya also stated that faith in the judiciary "would prevent these protests from tipping over into a popular revolution which unseats the government."
Nevertheless, she said, sustained discontent "might come to bite the government in 2029... or before that in the state elections."
It could also erode Modi's popularity, which has been a defining feature of Indian politics over the past decade, the expert indicated.
For Mukhopadhyay, the most troubling aspect of the current protests is the erosion of the electoral body's credibility.
Recalling the pride he felt when he registered to vote at 21, he drew comparisons with young Indian voters today. "The youngsters are now fighting for their vote."
Grad student accused of trying to flee U.S. after police questioned her about alleged poisoning
Microbiology grad student alleged to have poisoned tea of University of Wyoming colleague

A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents, then tried to flee the U.S. after police questioned her.

Aili Wang, 32, was arrested Oct. 6 at Los Angeles International Airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return to China. With her were "multiple" laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police.

Investigators say Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the alleged victim, who specialized in technology for disease treatment — research similar to work Wang had done in China.
Wang remained jailed without bail Tuesday in Los Angeles.
It's claimed the poison was first detected when the wife of the alleged victim and others tested water from the coffee maker he used to brew tea.
The microbiology professor overseeing both graduate students, Mark Gomelsky, said the accusations have left him reeling. He said he was uncertain if the alleged victim will fully recover.

"It's been disheartening, to say the least, to see that one of your student's life is in jeopardy and another student may be responsible for that," Gomelsky told The Associated Press. "That was one of the worst shocks in my professional career."
Wang has no attorney listed in court documents. The Associated Press tried to reach her via email and LinkedIn messages.

The police investigation began after the victim, identified in court documents as K.T., began experiencing symptoms and his wife and others allegedly isolated the chemical acrylamide in the coffee maker's water.
K.T. and campus police then set up surveillance cameras in the office space he shared with Wang at the university in Laramie, Wyo.

Wang allegedly was recorded Sept. 27 going through K.T.'s desk. On Oct. 1, she was recorded "taking photos and manipulating notebooks" on his desk, as well as rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug, a University of Wyoming campus police officer's affidavit said.
Wang and the alleged victim, who did not share research areas, did not get along, according to the affidavit.
Police said Wang had asked eBay to delete her account after she bought acrylamide over the online retail site twice last summer.
A carcinogenic byproduct of cooking starchy food and burning tobacco, acrylamide, which can be acutely toxic in high doses, is also used in microbiology research involving proteins or DNA.
During an interview by campus police on Oct. 5, Wang allegedly said she "had not used acrylamide in years."

A day later she was taken into custody in Los Angeles while in possession of "multiple laptops, multiple portable external digital storage devices, related accessories, physical records and written materials," according to a request by Wyoming prosecutors to "significantly increase" her $200,000 US bond upon extradition.

Wang had no reason to go through the desk of the other student whose federally funded, patent-pending research involved "new technology for cancer, neurological and genetic disease treatment," according to the affidavit.
Wang "was reportedly working on similar research in China before coming to the U.S.," the affidavit alleges.
Gomelsky described the alleged victim as a highly successful student from Vietnam.

Wang failed her first attempt to defend her dissertation and became envious of her colleague's success in discovering how to deliver RNA to human cells using bacteria, Gomelsky told The Associated Press.
The alleged victim began experiencing extreme tiredness, inability to sleep and other unexplained symptoms soon after attending a conference in August, Gomelsky said.
Later that month he went to the campus health clinic with worsening finger tingling and numbness, and leg weakness.
The student also said he had noticed a strange taste in the tea that he made with a small coffee maker on his desk, Gomelsky said, and that when he washed the coffee maker the taste would go away.
Suspecting someone in their shared office could be poisoning the student, Gomelsky said a chemistry professor tested the water and identified acrylamide.

The water from the coffee maker was boiled down to isolate 63 milligrams of white powder that tested positive for acrylamide, according to the affidavit. The amateur investigators turned the sample over to university police.

Discovery of the substance immediately made Tak Sumaya, an assistant professor who helped identify it in the coffee maker water, suspicious. Acrylamide is "not something you would find in that kind of quantity anywhere," Sumaya said.
The alleged victim was working on "a pretty promising cancer therapy method," Sumaya added.
The alleged victim continues to experience symptoms from the poisoning, including not being able to focus, tiring easily and a loss of sensation in his left hand, Gomelsky said.
"Acrylamide is a neurotoxin that cannot be neutralized so it stays in neurons and basically kills them. So it's unclear if he'll fully recover or not," the professor said.
Wang faces a felony aggravated assault and battery charge in Wyoming punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a $10,000 US fine.
It's not clear when she could be extradited to the state, where Albany County Circuit Court Judge Robert Sanford granted prosecutors' request and raised bond to $1.5 million US, cash only.

An inaugural, albeit short, White House press briefing offered a glimpse into how Trump's latest press secretary, Katie Zacharia, will approach the notoriously difficult role.
The 41-year-old spent much of the 14-minute appearance reading from prepared remarks before taking just three questions, all from conservative-leaning outlets.
Zacharia's debut comes after the departure of Karoline Leavitt, who became known for her combative and high-profile briefing style.

Zacharia, a conservative commentator named to the role on Friday, opened her first session by reading, at a notably slow pace, a lengthy list of what she described as achievements made by the "energetic" US President Donald Trump.
She highlighted Trump's recent campaign rallies and his policies on energy, tariffs, immigration and more since he returned to office.
"Everyday Americans are showing up in droves to attend rallies because of President Trump's America-first agenda of lower taxes, higher wages and one of my favourites, secure borders," Zacharia said.
"Attendance is at record highs as enthusiastic and hardworking Americans are lining up and packing arenas to support President Trump and Republicans.
"It's not hard to see why. President Trump is fighting and delivering for American workers every minute of every day."
Typically, a lengthy question-and-answer session follows a press secretary's opening remarks, often spanning dozens of questions from reporters.
But Zacharia took questions from just three reporters, starting with right-wing website Breitbart, an outlet frequently accused of misinformation.
The next questions went to Fox News and the Daily Mail.
When asked by Fox whether the administration had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine, Zacharia was unable to provide an answer.

Zacharia raised eyebrows when she was asked about her legal qualifications on the White House South Lawn alongside Trump after the briefing.

Trump turned to Zacharia and repeated the question.
A White House official later did not directly answer questions about whether Zacharia had passed a US bar exam, which is required in the US to practice law.

Pepperdine University confirmed Zacharia graduated from its law school in 2011, but there has been no confirmation so far she passed the California bar exam.
The briefing drew criticism from several former White House officials, who questioned both its length and Zacharia's performance.
Former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci joked on X: "The clock is running. Thus far 1/11th of a Scaramucci."

Sarah Matthews, who served as deputy White House press secretary during Trump's first term, described the debut as "rather underwhelming".

Scottie Scheffler continues to be the dominant world No 1 in men's golf, but how long will he stay top of the rankings and will he put more of Tiger Woods' records under threat?

Scheffler remains the most recent addition to the list of 25 players to have topped the Official World Golf Ranking (OWGR) since its introduction in 1986, with the American having four different spells at No 1 so far in his career.

The latest spell remains unbroken since May 2023, with Scheffler - as of October 12 - entering his 178th consecutive week as world No 1 and with a larger advantage over world No 2 Rory McIlroy than the Northern Irishman has over almost every active professional.

How do the rankings work and why is Scheffler so far ahead?
The world rankings run over a rolling two-year cycle, with points awarded based on the strength of that tournament's field and how high a player finishes on the leaderboard.

A golfer's world ranking then comes from dividing the number of points earned by the number of tournaments someone has played during the cycle, while bonus ranking points are given to players who have won multiple events in a 52-week period.

Scheffler registered two major wins among his six worldwide titles in 2025 and already has three victories in 2026, a campaign in which his remarkable consistency has seen him post top-three finishes in half of his 20 worldwide starts.

"He's the best player in the world by a country mile," said Sky Sports' Andrew Coltart. "It's his distance control and his ability to get scoring irons pin-high basically all the time, along with an incredible level of consistency.
"Also, very importantly, I think it's his golfing IQ and his understanding of how his game is and where his game is at - that's why he's the dominant force in the game."
How has Scheffler cemented himself as No 1?

Claiming his first three PGA Tour titles in a seven-week stretch saw Scheffler take top spot for the first time in March 2022, a fortnight before his maiden major victory at The Masters, a position he held until McIlroy overtook him that October.

Scheffler enjoyed a one-week burst back at the top after his 2023 WM Phoenix Open win and another four-week run after winning The Players the following month, before Jon Rahm leapfrogged him with his second major win secured at Augusta National.
Rahm would lose top spot when Scheffler tied-second at the PGA Championship a month later, with no player since able to end his ever-increasing reign as world No 1.

"He has managed to stay at the top for so long because he has no weaknesses across his game," Sky Sports' Nick Dougherty said. "He was once a below-average putter, but he's now world class and a top-10 putter.

"The iron play is peerless - he's not just the best, he's the best by a mile when he's at his very peak. He leads birdie average and leads bogey avoidance. When you look at all of that together, there's just a reason he's better than everyone in every area."

Only Woods and Greg Norman have spent longer in their careers at world No 1 than Scheffler, who aged just 30 has already won 22 PGA Tour titles - including four majors and three legs of the career Grand Slam - and cemented his status among the greats.

Woods was world No 1 for 281 consecutive weeks from June 2005 to October 2010, breaking his own record of 264 weeks previously held from August 1999 to September 2004, with Scheffler the closest to ever seriously threaten those historic runs.

Scheffler would need to remain in top spot until October 2035 to overtake Woods' career total of 683 weeks as No 1 but only until mid-October 2028 to break the longest consecutive spell, although he has plenty of work to do to reach that milestone.

"I have absolutely no valid reason why he won't [pass 281 weeks], when you look at what he's doing right now, but the level rises around you," Dougherty added. "Whether it's Rory coming back for him again or whether he has a little bit of a slump.

"Golf is just really hard to be that good for that long. Other than Tiger Woods we've never really seen it, other than Scheffler. There's new kids on the block too and they're all hungry, so I've got a feeling someone will get to him before then."

Dame Laura Davies added: "No [he won't break the record], because of the challenging pack behind him. It won't be that he necessarily drops off that much, I just think there's way too many good players just in behind him. Over two years, it's a long time."
Will Woods or McIlroy ever return to world No 1?
Woods is currently listed as 'unranked' in the OWGR standings, having not played an official event since The Open in July 2024 and only completed four 72-hole tournaments over the last six seasons.

The 50-year-old has previously ruled out a return to full-time professional golf and is unlikely to ever return to being one of the world's best, but McIlroy has continued to be Scheffler's closest challenger to the No 1 spot.

McIlroy has been no lower than third in the world rankings since Scheffler became No 1 and has been second since last March, with the Northern Irishman winning back-to-back Masters titles over the last two seasons.

"I think McIlroy still has another stint there [at No 1] because, when he's at his absolute strength, he is definitely alongside Scheffler," Dougherty insisted. "I think he can take him on his day, he just isn't as consistent as Scottie."
Coltart added: "For McIlroy to get back to world No 1 is really tough. He's at a different stage of his life and he's attained, arguably, what he ever set out in his life to attain.

"He's older, he's got different aspirations. I don't think the fire is necessarily there that it was in his belly when he was in his early 20s. It will be very difficult for Rory to do that and I hope that he proves me wrong."
Who is likely to be Scheffler's replacement?

Matt Fitzpatrick has moved to world No 3 after winning four times in 2026, although the Zurich Classic of New Orleans did not offer world ranking points, while Players champion Cameron Young and US Open winner Wyndham Clark complete the top five.

Scheffler previously jumped from world No 15 to world No 1 in a six-week burst in 2022, highlighting that rapid rises are possible, although any of his challengers would likely require multiple more victories to be next in line for the world No 1 spot.

"If it's not Rory to go past him, it's hard to imagine who it would be among this current crop," Dougherty admitted. "It could be someone like Jackson Koivun, who is a new arrival and he's a superstar that clearly stands out already.
"It could be one of these young guns, it could even be someone we don't know yet, that's going to displace him at the top of the game."
Chris Gotterup, Sam Burns and Si Woo Kim have also made big rises up the world rankings in 2026, while Koivun and Miles Russell are others tipped to have big futures on the PGA Tour.

"There's half a dozen of them that could string together results, because that's what world No 1 is all about - consistency," Davies said. "At some point, someone will go past him. Who will that be? We'll have to wait and see.
"Watch this space, because they're all very good. He [Scheffler] is just that little bit better at the moment."

A hundred in the warm-up match prior to the series promised much, as did his pair of 37s in this Test before failing to convert either into a score of note - let alone a century.

Averaging only 25.29 with the bat in his 24 Tests played since last topping three figures at Old Trafford in the 2023 Ashes, Labuschagne was considered incrediblly fortunate to keep his place in this Australian side but it came as a result of a lack of alternative options staking a claim.

Maddinson last played Test cricket for Australia in late 2016, averaging 6.75 across his three appearances, with his career since stalled by injury, mental health issues, and then a testicular cancer diagnosis that sidelined him for most of last year.
As a result, the 34-year-old hadn't played a first-class match since March 2025 before returning to the Test team in Durban after injuries to other batting options Cameron Green and Josh Inglis.

His first-innings 33-ball duck was an inauspicious start to his second coming in international cricket, and though he played with a great deal more freedom in the second innings, with Australia well ahead of the game by that stage - striking six fours and a couple of sixes in his 48 off 38 balls - his place in the team will continue to come under scrutiny.
Especially as Green and Inglis are now set to be back available for the second Test in Gqeberha.

To jettison Maddison after only one game back would be incredibly harsh, but Australia will be eager to get golden-boy Green, in particular, back into the team - and Renshaw has blocked his most obvious route for return at No 5.
Could he come in for Labuschagne at No 3, or Beau Webster at No 7 after he was underused as an all-rounder here? There's still much to be resolved with the look of this batting line-up.
Hazlewood and co prove they're still a force
If there was one aspect of Australia's performance that should concern England, however, it's the continued quality and depth of their bowling attack.

Josh Hazlewood's career-best Test figures of 6-49 in the second innings completed a dominant performance by the visiting seamers. Skipper Pat Cummins had led the attack first time around, taking 3-54 to help dismiss South Africa for a below-par 284 on a decent batting deck.
The evergreen talents of 38-year-old off-spinner Nathan Lyon add a further dimension, while Australia also boast Scott Boland and Michael Neser in reserve.

That depth will matter over the coming months. Australia's attack is an ageing group, and the demands of an intense Test schedule - a four-match series at home to New Zealand and five away in India - following the trip to South Africa will test their fitness and durability.
How will they be holding up by the time the Ashes comes around on June 18 with the first Test at Trent Bridge?
For the time being though, any optimistic talk of Australia's attack being past their best by then looks massively premature.
South Africa team selection a head-scratcher
South Africa's team selection for the series opener raised some questions, particularly the decision to field two specialist spinners in Durban.

Keshav Maharaj and Simon Harmer offered a left and right-arm option, but neither proved particularly potent, with just the four wickets shared between them - including only one in the first innings, to Harmer's name, allowing Australia to recover from 124-6 to post 390.

The absence of Kagiso Rabada, having failed to recover from a hamstring injury in time for this Test, perhaps forced the selectors' hand, but it left their attack looking a little lopsided and somewhat patched together.
Wiaan Mulder, for example, should not be operating with the new ball in Test cricket.
The batting all-rounder took two wickets with it on the first morning, and burgled a couple more into day two, but was pretty ineffective otherwise for his 31 overs of hard toil through the Test.

The return of Anrich Nortje was encouraging. After an extended absence from Test cricket, the fast bowler showed glimpses of the pace and aggression that made him a major asset during his first stint in the side from 2019 to 2023.
And assuming Rabada is back fit and available for the second Test in Gqeberha, his return would provide greater balance and potency to South Africa's attack.
The prospect of Rabada, Nortje and the left-arm option of Marco Jansen steaming in would represent a much sterner challenge for Australia, and England in a couple months' time.

Yemen: Houthi siege, cholera outbreak and aid cuts put civilians in the crosshairs

Yemen’s southwestern city of Taiz is facing a “devastating” humanitarian crisis as escalating tensions are dramatically driving up food prices and causing shortages of supplies, the UN Spokesperson said on Tuesday.
Taiz, Yemen’s third largest city, has been a major battleground between the Iran-backed Houthis and the internationally recognised Saudi-backed Yemeni government since the start of the war in 2014.
The Houthis have besieged the city since 2015 but tightened their blockade at the start of this month when they took control of the last main road between Taiz and other government-held areas.
The development is part of a broader offensive the Houthis launched in early September to seize key territory along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast.

Current wheat and flour supplies in Taiz could run out in less than three weeks, while food prices have reportedly risen about 50 per cent and cooking gas has become largely unavailable, the UN warns.
Petrol prices have also tripled and fuel shortages are putting water supply and health services at risk.

“We continue to urge [the parties] to…uphold their obligations under international humanitarian law and to refrain from direct attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure and take constant care to spare both civilians and the infrastructure they use,” The UN’s Stéphane Dujarric stressed on Tuesday.
At the same time, across the country, escalating conflict and mass displacement have disrupted health services and pushed people into overcrowded shelters with inadequate access to safe water.
As a consequence, Yemen is seeing a surge in cholera – an acute and potentially fatal intestinal infection, which mostly spreads through water or food contaminated by human faeces.
The country has reported 8,034 suspected cholera cases and 27 deaths this year, with a quarter of them occurring in the last four weeks.
Since August, 200,000 people have been displaced, which the UN’s health organization WHO notes coincides with a sharp increase in cholera transmission.
Children also face serious risks from measles, with more than 22,800 suspected cases and 128 deaths reported this year.
Vaccination coverage, at an estimated 45 per cent for each of the two recommended doses, is critically low in Yemen, increasing the risk of outbreaks of vaccine-preventable diseases.
Health facilities, which are already treating thousands of people injured in the fighting, are struggling to keep up with the growing disease burden.
Approximately 500 health facilities across nine affected governorates lack partner support, the WHO found.

The agency is working with the Yemeni government to strengthen surveillance, testing and treatment, but its 90-day emergency response is critically underfunded. It needs $31 million and has received just $4.3 million, less than 14 per cent of the total.

“Without urgent funding and unimpeded access to safe water, vaccination and essential health services, outbreaks could spread rapidly among already vulnerable communities,” said WHO official Dr Annette Heinzelmann.
800 million young people face a future without jobs

Approximately 800 million young people entering the labour market in developing economies over the coming years will not find jobs unless countries act, the head of the UN Development Programme (UNDP) warned on Tuesday, as the agency launched two initiatives to boost investment and employment.

“If you look at the next 15 years, there will be 1.2 billion young people graduating from school, going into the labour market,” UNDP Administrator Alexander De Croo told a press briefing in New York from Bangkok, where he is attending the World Bank Group-International Monetary Fund (IMF) Annual Meetings.
“Unfortunately, for only 400 million of these, there will be jobs. For 800 million of these, there will not be jobs.”
Mr. De Croo said the gap was driven by demographics – in many developing countries, the median age is between 18 and 25 – and that the job projections were based on the current state of technology.
“That is not going to go by itself. This is the result of policy,” he said.

Of the two initiatives, the Investment Accelerator will help governments improve investment policies and legal frameworks, build pipelines of investment-ready projects and move them from preparation to implementation.
The Jobs for Prosperity Facility will help countries identify sectors with strong job-creation potential, align skills with what employers need and tackle barriers to business investment and hiring.

Asked whether artificial intelligence (AI) was a factor, Mr. De Croo said the projections could change through active labour policies, noting that sectors such as care, agriculture and tourism would still create many jobs even as AI accelerates.
“Job creation is actually the only real sustainable way for people to grow out of poverty,” he said.

Both initiatives are backed by expanded partnerships with the World Bank Group, the European Investment Bank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, with pilot initiatives already underway in Nepal, Yemen, Haiti, Lebanon and Ghana.
The launch comes as many developing countries face what Mr. De Croo called a “triple shock”: high energy costs, one of the most pronounced El Niño events since 1950, and very high borrowing costs.
According to a new UNDP report, No Time to Recover, the median developing country now spends 9.5 per cent of total government income on interest payments alone.
For the first time since 2010, the number of people living in multidimensional poverty – which measures not only income but also access to electricity, water, health care and education – has risen.
“Those numbers should absolutely be a wake-up call to all of us,” Mr. De Croo said.
While the global economy has proved more resilient than expected, that resilience is not shared equally, he added.
“Some countries have still quite strong economic fundamentals. Others do not have the fundamentals to withstand further shocks.”
